newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS -Payrolls may bring US down to earth.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS -Payrolls may bring US down to earth.

text.p: Investors would be well advised to take short positions in U.S. Treasuries near term, as risks remain firmly skewed to the downside going into key June payrolls data on Thursday, analysts said.
With the market already convinced interest rates will remain on hold after Wednesday's FOMC meeting, the scope for a relief rally is limited, they said.
Combine that with the danger of a stronger-than-expected payrolls number on Thursday, and the market will be hard-pushed to gain ground.

"The fact it's a uniform consensus that there'll be no rate rise suggests the way to trade would be to go short this week purely on the basis that the only surprise will be on the downside," said David Hewitt, bond strategist at Tokyo Mitsubishi International.
According to a Reuter poll, economists expect June non-farm payrolls to rise by 222,000 on Thursday after a gain of 138,000 in May.
"I would err on the high side (for June payrolls) as a payback for the low number we saw in May," said Dick Howard, senior economist at Bank Julius Baer. He expected a figure closer to 275,000.
"I have a nasty feeling we could be in for an earnings surprise with the last few months better than expected," he added.
But the U.S. Independence Day holiday on Friday should mute any negative fall-out from a strong payrolls number, limiting the chances of a dramatic sell-off.
Longer term, analysts said the U.S. Treasury curve was in danger of becoming a touch complacent in its interest rate outlook.
Howard said he was convinced the Fed would have to raise interest rates during the second half of the year, probably by 50 basis points.
"So the whole curve looks expensive to me. Our end of year forecast sees the short and long end rising by 50 basis points at both ends."

Howard said to make the best of such an outlook, investors should plump for the short end of the Treasury curve, as prices at that end tend to fall less than at the long end when the whole yield curve shifts up.
Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at Bank America in London, agreed the market's hopes for a soft landing for the U.S. economy may slightly overdone.
"It does seem as if a lot of good news is priced in now," he said. "The risks in the economy are still on the upside...with a reasonable possibility of a rebound in spending in the next few months."

And with the economy nearing full capacity, any such acceleration would have little room for manoeuvre, said Hawkins, leaving market expectations of an ideal world of low inflation and steady growth optimistic.
"It may be the case, but I think the risks are very much stacked in the other direction," said Hawkins.

He said 30-year cash bond yields may tick up after the payrolls data, depending on whether they come in stronger-than-expected. He said the yield may rise to around 6.80,85 percent next week from their present 6.73 percent.

The 10-year T-bond/Bund spread may also suffer temporarily if payrolls surprise to the upside, said Hawkins. He said a move to 100 basis points on the spread was possible, from its present 90 basis points.
